title: Give or take: more vague expressions
subtitle: in excess of, give or take, a dash of, or whatever
summary: Be deliberately imprecise about numbers, quantities and things - in excess of, in the region of, give or take, a smattering, a dollop, or something along those lines.

lesson.heading: Vague expressions for numbers
rows: in excess of
more than; used in more formal contexts
He left a sum in excess of $1 million when he died.
in the region of
around, about; less formal
It'll cost you somewhere in the region of £900 a month to rent a flat.
give or take
a little more or a little less; informal
It'll take five hours, give or take half an hour, to drive there.
approximately
about; rather formal
The second meeting is approximately two and a half months after the first one.
a week or so
more than a week, but unclear how much more; informal
It'll take a week or so to get the computer repaired.
quite a few
a surprisingly or undesirably large number
Quite a few students hadn't registered.

lesson.heading: Vague expressions for quantities
rows: a smattering of
a small proportion
There was only a smattering of women authors among the prize winners.
a dash / a smidgen of
a very small quantity
Would you like a dash of chilli sauce with your kebab?
a dollop of
usually a small amount, though you can also say a large dollop
I'd like a dollop of ice cream with my fruit salad.
stacks of
a large number or quantity of; informal
I used to have stacks of CDs, but now I have them all on one memory stick.

lesson.heading: More or less; a bit
lesson.text: **More or less** goes with verbs and adverbs to make things vaguer. **A bit** and **a bit of a** go with adjectives and nouns to soften the meaning.

examples.text: I think we've **more or less** solved the problem with the computer now.
My English is **more or less** the same level as the other students in the class.
I'm **a bit** fed up with all the complaints I'm getting.
We were in **a bit of a** panic when we heard there was a strike at the airport.

lesson.note: We do not usually use more or less with people's ages.

lesson.heading: Referring vaguely to things and actions
rows: or whatever
or similar activities
You could spend Sunday going to museums or galleries or whatever.
or something
or any other thing of that type
If you don't want tea, have a lemonade or something.
and things like that / and that kind of thing
and other similar things
In the evenings we played board games and things like that.
or something along those lines
something fitting that description
We need a big plastic container; a dustbin or something along those lines would do.
or words to that effect
or similar words expressing the same meaning
He said he was fed up with all the criticisms, or words to that effect.

lesson.heading: More vague items you will hear in conversation
rows: sort of / kind of
with adjectives and almost any other word class
Her hair's a sort of reddish colour. / a kind of elasticky thing
-ish
on adjectives, ages and clock times
She's forty, forty-fourish. / We arrived around half-past sevenish.
a bit on the ... side
with adjectives, for a quality that is not what we hoped for
The garden was a bit on the big side. / The living room was a bit on the dark side.
-y on a noun or adjective
to make it less precise; very informal
It was a browny colour with a kind of acidy taste.
and that
and similar things; very informal
They're comfortable on long walks and that.
and suchlike
and similar things; usually after a plural noun
I've had treatments and suchlike.

lesson.text: In excess of and approximately belong in a report; give or take, or whatever and and that belong in the pub.

exercises.prompt: Make it vaguer and formal: The company will invest ___ £10 million in new technology over the next five years.
exercises.explanation: In excess of is the formal way of saying more than.

exercises.prompt: Make it vaguer and less formal: It will cost you ___ £10,000 to have the whole house redecorated.
exercises.explanation: In the region of is a less formal way of saying approximately.

exercises.prompt: Make it informal: It could take seven hours, ___ an hour, to drive to Aberdeen.
exercises.hint: (three words: a little more or less)
exercises.explanation: Give or take an hour means it could be an hour more or an hour less.

exercises.prompt: Make it vaguer: ___ students failed the exam. I was rather surprised and disappointed.
exercises.explanation: Quite a few means a surprisingly or undesirably large number.

exercises.prompt: Just a ___ of milk in my coffee, please. I like it quite dark.
exercises.hint: (a very small quantity; two possible words)
exercises.explanation: A dash or a smidgen of something is a very small quantity.

exercises.prompt: Most of the people in the class were Spanish, with just a ___ of other nationalities.
exercises.explanation: A smattering of something is a small proportion of it.

exercises.prompt: She put a ___ of mayonnaise on her salad and mixed it all up.
exercises.explanation: A dollop is usually a small amount, though you can also have a large dollop.

exercises.prompt: He put ___ of hair gel on before going out to the party.
exercises.explanation: Stacks of something is an informal way of saying a large number or quantity of it.

exercises.prompt: It's a ___ worrying that she hasn't rung. I hope she's not ill.
exercises.hint: (two words used to soften an adjective)
exercises.explanation: A bit softens an adjective; a bit of a softens a noun.

exercises.prompt: The computer keeps crashing; it's a bit of a ___ .
exercises.explanation: A bit of a is used to soften a noun such as nuisance, pain or problem.

exercises.prompt: There were six of us working, so we'd ___ finished by 5 pm.
exercises.hint: (three words used with verbs to make them vaguer)
exercises.explanation: More or less makes a verb or adverb less precise.

exercises.prompt: Match each vague item with what it does.

pairs.right: used with adjectives for a quality that is not what we hoped for
added to an adjective, an age or a clock time
and similar things, normally after a plural noun
or similar words with the same meaning

options: He's in excess of 35 or whatever.
exercises.explanation: We do not usually use more or less with people's ages - use about.

exercises.prompt: Complete informally: 'It's a sort of craft shop; they sell souvenirs ___ .'
exercises.explanation: And things like that (or and that kind of thing) refers vaguely to other similar items.

exercises.prompt: 'We need a big container made of plastic; a dustbin ___ would do.' Which phrase fits?
exercises.explanation: Something along those lines means something fitting that description.

exercises.statement: 'It'll take a week or so' means it will take slightly less than a week.
exercises.explanation: It means more than a week, but it is not clear how much more.

exercises.prompt: Which of these vague expressions would be acceptable in formal writing, and which are informal only?
Put this vague sentence in order.
exercises.answer: It'll take five hours, give or take half an hour
exercises.explanation: Give or take half an hour means it could take four and a half or five and a half hours.
